 by Agence France-Presse , Sakina Abidi Published:  10:30pm, 01 Nov 2026 Length: 674 words LISTEN TO THIS ARTICLE PRINT SHARE Hunters gather to celebrate a 700-year-old tradition known as Miss de Diobaye, which marks the beginning of the rainy season in the village of Ndiaye Ndiaye in southwest Senegal. Photo: AFP
 Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you. 
 This week’s podcast is voiced by Ambrose Li, a reporter on SCMP’s Hong Kong desk, and Young Post deputy editor Esther Cheung. 
 SCMP Young Post · Listen: Senegalese hunt beckons the rain (adapted from AFP, voiced by Ambrose Li and Esther Cheung) 
 Script 
 Adapted from Agence France-Presse 
 Voice 1: Against a frenzy of drums, chanting and gunfire, a few hundred Serer men paraded about in a dreamlike state. They showed off the day’s hunt – jackals, monitor lizards, monkeys and birds. The hunt and this ritual were done in hopes of hastening Senegal’s rainy season.
 Voice 2: Senegal, like other countries in Africa’s Sahel region, has a typically hot and dry climate with a rainy season. In Ndiaye Ndiaye, a village in southwest Senegal, an annual hunt is held to bring rain and protect the community. This centuries-old tradition, held this year in July, is known as the Miss de Diobaye.
 Voice 1: The ritual belongs to the country’s Serer ethnic minority group and heralds the start of the farming season. But in recent years, the hunt has been disrupted by deforestation and modernisation. Climate change is also causing the rains to arrive later.
 Voice 2: On his motorbike, a firefighter returned from his seventh Diobaye hunt. He came with eight other young men, riding in the scorching heat. He explained how the men chased the animals on motorbikes. The hunters shared the catch, hacking it with machetes and finally hanging it from their belts.
 Voice 1: Men in the community must undergo initiation rites before they are allowed to take part in the mystical hunt. The day before the event, a traditional seer predicts which animal must be killed to trigger abundant rain. The secret is shared only among the initiates.
 Voice 2: Legend says the practice began seven centuries ago during a terrible drought, when a seer foretold the return of rain only if a specific animal was killed. On the evening the animal was hunted down, heavy rain fell on Ndiaye Ndiaye, bringing a bountiful harvest and the birth of a tradition.
 Voice 1: The young men’s return to the district was marked by a spirited procession with drums and chanting. The hunters bashed their machetes and fired their rifles and pistols to ward off evil spirits. From a safe distance, women and children were generally in high spirits – though sometimes startled by the gunfire – as they watched the parade.
 Voice 2: Miss de Diobaye is a moment of emotional relief entrusted to the youngest men, said Sobel Dione, an anthropologist who specialises in Serer culture. As the parade drew to a close, hunters gathered by their families to dance before traditional and religious leaders and state officials, waving their weapons.
 Voice 1: Over the centuries, the Miss de Diobaye has had to adapt. Hunting methods shifted with the introduction of motorbikes. The once vast forest has been reduced to a sprawling plain with few trees, depleted by human-driven deforestation. The antelopes and rhinos once hunted by ancestors no longer exist in the region. Peanut and millet farming practices have also changed, with new seed varieties that mature more quickly.
 Voice 2: Today, climate change has further modified the tradition, with the rains arriving increasingly later and for shorter periods. Sitor Ndour, secretary general of the Miss de Diobaye organising committee, noted that the timing of the hunt had shifted over the decades. It used to be held in May, which was when the rainy season would have set in.
 Voice 1: History will show that in 2026, the day after the Miss de Diobaye, western Senegal did receive the season’s first major rainfall.
